title: Sentence Screen Fitting
summary: Determine how many times a given sentence, with words in their original order and no splitting, can fit on a screen defined by rows and columns, ensuring each word occupies a separate space.
statement: Determine how many times a given sentence, with words in their original order and no splitting, can fit on a screen defined by rows and columns, ensuring each word occupies a separate space.
constraints: 1 <= sentence.length <= 100; each word has 1–10 lowercase English letters.
1 <= rows, cols <= 20,000. Words keep their cyclic sentence order and cannot split across lines.
Use one space between words on the same line; no leading or required trailing space. Count complete sentence repetitions only.
reference_solution:
def sentence_screen_count(sentence, rows, cols):
    count = len(sentence)
    cycle_width = sum(len(word)+1 for word in sentence)
    cycles,remaining = divmod(cols+1,cycle_width)
    transitions = []
    for start in range(count):
        used,extra = 0,0
        while used+len(sentence[(start+extra)%count])+1<=remaining:
            used += len(sentence[(start+extra)%count])+1
            extra += 1
        words = cycles*count+extra
        transitions.append(((start+words)%count,(start+words)//count))
    index,total = 0,0
    for _ in range(rows):
        index,completed = transitions[index]
        total += completed
    return total

hints: Only the next word index needs to carry across row boundaries.
Precompute how many complete sentences and what next index one row produces from each starting word.
Treat each word as length+1 and give the row cols+1 space; take whole cycles, then scan the remaining partial cycle.
The extra virtual column cancels only the final trailing space. Whole-cycle arithmetic makes preprocessing O(n^2), then rows take O(rows).
editorial: Add a virtual trailing space to every placed word and one virtual column to the row. A whole cyclic sentence costs the same width from any starting index. Fit as many cycles as possible, then fewer than n extra words. Store the resulting index and number of wraps. Applying these transitions row by row handles continuation and words wider than a row without splitting words.
